cards.body: Columns are letters, rows are numbers, and a cell is where they meet: B7. A range is a rectangle: A1:C10 means everything from A1 down-right to C10. Once you think in addresses, formulas stop feeling like magic.
cards.title: Every sheet is a grid — learn its address system

cards.body: Write =A1*2 in B1 and copy it down — B2 becomes =A2*2. That's relative: it shifts with the cell. Add dollar signs to lock it: =$A$1*2 always points at A1, no matter where you paste it. Mixing them ($A1 or A$1) locks one axis only.
cards.title: Relative references move; absolute references don't

cards.body:
Price list in A2:A10, tax rate in B1. In C2 write =A2*$B$1 — the A2 slides down each row while $B$1 stays glued to the tax rate. Fill down and every row computes correctly.
Memory trick: the dollar signs are 'nails' pinning the reference in place.
Never type the same number into ten formulas. Put it in one cell, reference it with $ signs, and change it once when it changes. One source of truth beats ten copies.

cards.explain: References are relative by default — they shift with the cell. A1 becomes A2 one row down. Dollar signs ($A$1) would have kept it locked.
cards.q: You copy =A1*2 from B1 down to B2. What does B2 contain?

questions.explain: Absolute references are nailed down — $B$2 never moves, wherever you paste it.
questions.q: =$B$2 copied from C5 to D7 still points at…

choices: Ten cells in column A, rows 2–10
questions.explain: A colon between two cells means the whole rectangle between them — here, ten cells.

choices: It tells the sheet 'compute this', not 'display this'
questions.explain: The equals sign switches the cell from text mode to formula mode. No =, no calculation.
questions.q: Why does every formula start with =?

questions.explain: The $ nails the column to A while the row stays relative — but moving one column right doesn't change the row, so it stays =$A1.

choices: Reference $B$1 everywhere — one cell to update
questions.explain: One source of truth: reference the cell with $ signs. When the rate changes, you edit one cell, not fifty formulas.
questions.q: Tax rate lives in B1 and you need it in 50 formulas. Best practice?

flashcards.back: A range: every cell from A1 down-right to C10.
An absolute reference — locked to A1 even when copied anywhere.
= (the equals sign). Without it, you're typing text, not math.
Copying a formula down a column — relative references adjust row by row.

cards.body: SUM adds a range, AVERAGE takes the mean, COUNT counts numbers (COUNTA counts non-empty cells too). They ignore text automatically. These three answer 80% of 'what does this column say?' questions.
cards.title: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT — the holy trinity

cards.body: =IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Example: =IF(A2>=60,"Pass","Fail"). IFs nest for multiple branches, but three nested IFs means you should switch to a lookup table instead — your future self will thank you.
cards.title: IF is a fork in the road

cards.body:
Grades in B2:B30. =AVERAGE(B2:B30) gives the class mean. =COUNTIF(B2:B30,">=90") counts A-students. =IF(AVERAGE(B2:B30)>=70,"Class passed","Class failed") turns the number into a verdict.
COUNTIF is COUNT with a condition — the pattern behind half of all reporting.
VLOOKUP is the old king; XLOOKUP is the new one. XLOOKUP defaults to exact match (no more surprise wrong answers) and looks left or right. If your sheet has XLOOKUP, use it and never look back.

cards.explain: 150 > 100 is true, so IF returns the second argument. The test decides; the branches just wait their turn.

questions.explain: (10+20+30)/3 = 20. AVERAGE divides the sum by how many numbers there are.
IF takes test first, then the true-branch, then the false-branch — in that order, always.
questions.q: You need 'Pass' if score ≥ 60 else 'Fail'. Correct formula?

choices: Exact match by default — no silent wrong answers
questions.explain: VLOOKUP's default approximate match quietly returns wrong results when the data isn't sorted. XLOOKUP defaults to exact.
questions.q: Why is XLOOKUP safer than VLOOKUP for beginners?

questions.explain: COUNT counts numbers only — text is ignored. (COUNTA would count all five non-empty cells.)
questions.q: =COUNT(A1:A5) where A1:A5 holds 3 numbers and 2 words returns…

questions.explain: Nested IFs rot fast. A small lookup table turns branching logic into data — readable, testable, editable.
questions.q: Three nested IFs are getting unreadable. Better move?

flashcards.back: Adds all numbers in A1 through A10.
Returns 'yes' when the test is true, 'no' when false.
Counts cells in the range that are 90 or above.
XLOOKUP defaults to exact match and searches any direction; VLOOKUP defaults to approximate and only looks right.

cards.body: Filters (Data → Filter) let you show only rows matching a condition without deleting anything. Sorting rearranges; filtering hides. Rule: filter to ask 'which rows?', sort to ask 'in what order?' — and never sort one column alone or you'll scramble your rows.
cards.title: Sort and filter before you analyze

cards.body: A pivot table summarizes thousands of rows in seconds: drag 'Region' to rows, 'Sales' to values, and you get totals per region. No formulas. Change the drag, change the question — it's the fastest way to explore a dataset you didn't build.
cards.title: Pivot tables: drag, drop, done

cards.body:
10,000 sales rows. Pivot: rows = Month, values = SUM of Revenue → monthly revenue in four drags. Add 'Product' to columns → a month-by-product grid. What took an afternoon of formulas takes a minute.
Pivot tables don't change your data — they just look at it from above.

Charts lie by default: truncated y-axes exaggerate tiny differences, and 3D pie charts distort every slice. Start every axis at zero unless you have a real reason, and prefer bars over pies — humans compare lengths far better than angles.

choices: Rows scramble — C no longer matches its row
cards.explain: Sorting one column detaches it from its rows — names no longer match their scores. Always sort with the whole table selected (or use Sort Range with headers).
cards.q: You sort column C alone in a 5-column table. What happens?

choices: A pivot table: Region to rows, Sales to values
A formula in each of 10,000 rows
questions.explain: Pivots summarize by dragging fields — four drags replace an afternoon of formulas, with zero formula errors.
questions.q: Fastest way to get total sales per region from 10,000 rows?

choices: Tiny differences look dramatic — likely misleading
questions.explain: Truncated axes magnify small gaps. Start at zero unless the data genuinely lives far from it.
questions.q: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 98 instead of 0. Effect?

choices: A filter on the Status column
questions.explain: Filters hide without deleting — the full data stays intact underneath. Deleting is for data you truly never need.
questions.q: You need only the rows where Status = 'Overdue'. Use…

choices: Rearranging the question takes seconds, not rewrites
questions.explain: Drag a field, get a new answer. Formulas need rewriting for every new question; pivots just need a new drag.
questions.q: Why do pivot tables beat formulas for exploring data?

questions.explain: Humans judge bar lengths far more accurately than pie angles — and 3D distorts both. Bars win for precision.
questions.q: Comparing 5 products' sales precisely — best chart?

flashcards.back: Filter hides non-matching rows; sort reorders all rows. Neither deletes data.
Drag-and-drop summary of big data: rows/columns define groups, values define the math.
Starting the axis above zero — makes tiny differences look huge. Usually deceptive.
Bars: humans compare lengths accurately. Pies: angles fool us — use bars for precision.
